title: Ada and the Room
premise: Elodie Amberdale, a pest controller who prides herself on explaining everything, is called to a house where the infestation leaves fingerprints in dust and flour. Waiting on the porch is Wren, her childhood imaginary friend, unchanged after thirty years, who claims Elodie witnessed something in 1974 that she was made to forget: a child taken by the town's founding family, buried beneath their orchard, with a whole community complicit in the silence. As Wren peels back the memory block by block, Elodie realizes the 'pests' are the unquiet dead of everyone the Ambersdales erased, and that her own family helped bury the truth. The law offers nothing—the perpetrators are dead or untouchable—so justice must come from witness: Elodie digs up what was taken, names it publicly, and lets the dead be seen. In the end she returns the stolen bones to the child's mother's grave, releases Wren from his long vigil, and accepts that being invisible to power was never safety—only silence.
about_author: Zephyrine Underhill spent a decade cataloguing county archives in rural England, where she developed an obsession with the crimes towns agree not to remember. She writes horror about ordinary people forced to become witnesses, and insists she has never had an imaginary friend—or that one has never had her.

chapters.title: The Call-Out
chapters.summary: Elodie's POV. A routine pest control job at Hollowmere House turns strange: droppings arranged in patterns, small handprints in the flour bin, claw marks too high for any animal. The client, elderly Mrs. Voss, won't meet her eyes. Emotional beat: professional skepticism curdling into unease as Elodie's rational explanations start requiring more faith than belief would.

chapters.title: Someone on the Porch
chapters.summary: Elodie's POV. Leaving at dusk, she finds a figure on the porch steps—a boy of eight in 1970s clothes, exactly as she drew him in crayon forty years ago. He says only, 'You promised you'd come back.' She drives away shaking. Emotional beat: terror braided with a homesickness she can't name; the past arriving punctual as a delivery.

chapters.title: Crayon Evidence
chapters.summary: Elodie's POV, intercut with memory fragments. At home she finds her childhood drawings of Wren in her mother's attic—and a page she doesn't remember drawing: a house, an orchard, a small shape under the soil. Her mother's handwriting on the back: 'Stop this. Stop asking.' Emotional beat: the first crack in her identity as someone who explains things.

chapters.title: What the Dust Says
chapters.summary: Elodie returns to Hollowmere professionally, telling herself it's about the contract. The fingerprints lead upstairs to a sealed nursery; inside, dust has settled into the outline of a child who isn't there. Wren appears in the mirror behind her. Emotional beat: dread shifting from 'is this real' to 'what did I do.'

chapters.title: Wren Explains Nothing
chapters.summary: Dual POV drifting between Elodie and Wren. Wren speaks in riddles of the time before: he was made to wait, he cannot leave the property line, he remembers 1974 perfectly because forgetting was done to the living, not the dead. Emotional beat: grief disguised as irritation; Elodie angry at him for existing, angrier at herself for being glad.

chapters.title: The Amberdale Name
chapters.summary: Elodie's POV. Researching Hollowmere's history at the county archive (where she once worked), she finds her own surname in the 1974 records: her father signed a statement about a missing child, then withdrew it. The archivist goes pale when she asks questions. Emotional beat: betrayal—the discovery that her family wasn't innocent bystander but participant.

chapters.title: Mrs. Voss Remembers Wrong
chapters.summary: Elodie's POV. She confronts Mrs. Voss, whose account of 1974 shifts with each telling, polished like a stone. Under pressure the old woman breaks: 'We all agreed. It was better for everyone.' Emotional beat: horror at how memory becomes a communal instrument; the banality of complicity.

chapters.title: Pests
chapters.summary: Wren's POV. The dead of Hollowmere are not ghosts but residue—people erased so thoroughly they persist as infestations, nesting in walls. Wren tends them like a groundskeeper. He shows Elodie the nursery wall where names were scratched and plastered over. Emotional beat: compassion for the monstrous; the dead are only frightening because the living made them so.

chapters.title: Nineteen Seventy-Four
chapters.summary: Elodie's POV, framed as recovered memory. The block breaks: a summer evening, the Amberdale orchard, her father holding a lantern, men from the Bramley family carrying something wrapped in sacking, seven-year-old Elodie watching from the hedge, told to forget. Emotional beat: vertigo and nausea; the body remembering what the mind was forbidden.

chapters.title: The Boy Who Was Taken
chapters.summary: Elodie's POV. The missing child was Thomas Fairburn, son of a woman the town declared unfit; the Bramleys 'adopted' him, he died within weeks, and the paperwork dissolved him. Wren was Thomas's imaginary friend first—made real by a dying boy's need, left behind. Emotional beat: heartbreak; Wren is not a haunting but an orphaned promise.

chapters.title: Invisible by Design
chapters.summary: Elodie's POV. She understands the theme plainly now: the powerful didn't hide the crime, they hid the victim—made him invisible, and made invisibility feel like safety to everyone else. She tries going to the police; the surviving Bramley heir is a magistrate. Emotional beat: fury at the law's blindness; the realization that official channels are part of the architecture.

chapters.title: Pressure in the Walls
chapters.summary: Multiple POVs. The residue grows restless as Elodie gets closer; Hollowmere's new owners report swarms, whispers, wet handprints. Mrs. Voss dies suddenly, leaving Elodie a key and a note: 'Orchard. Third row. I'm sorry I waited so long.' Emotional beat: accelerating dread; the deadline made physical.

chapters.title: The Key
chapters.summary: Elodie's POV. The key opens a disused well-house on the old Bramley estate. Inside: boxes of Thomas's things—shoes, drawings, a tooth kept as a trophy—that prove he existed. Also letters showing her father was paid for his silence. Emotional beat: grief weaponized into resolve; evidence without a court that will hear it.

chapters.title: They Know You're Digging
chapters.summary: Elodie's POV. Threats arrive: slashed tires, a visit from the Bramley heir, a lawyer citing trespass and defamation against a dead child. Someone burns the archive box. But burning paper doesn't burn memory, and Wren can show her everything. Emotional beat: isolation hardening into defiance; power corrupting on schedule.

chapters.title: What Wren Was For
chapters.summary: Wren's POV. He confesses his purpose: imaginary friends hold what children can't carry. Thomas gave him his memories before dying so someone would keep them. Wren has waited fifty years for a living person strong enough to receive them back. Emotional beat: devastating tenderness; love as a container for testimony.

chapters.title: Taking It Back
chapters.summary: Elodie's POV. In the nursery, Wren transfers the full memory—not just the burial but Thomas's last days, his voice, his fear, his jokes. Elodie carries it without flinching, becoming the witness the town refused to be. Emotional beat: the cost of witnessing made flesh; she weeps for a boy she never met and will never forget.

chapters.title: Third Row
chapters.summary: Elodie's POV, night. With the key, the memory, and a borrowed excavator permit forged by a sympathetic former colleague, she digs in the orchard. The Bramley heir arrives with men. The ground itself seems to object—roots moving, cold rising. Emotional beat: climax tension; the living trying to stop what the earth has waited to give up.

chapters.title: Small Bones
chapters.summary: Elodie's POV. They find him. The heir orders her arrested; instead, the assembled residue of Hollowmere's erased dead manifests fully for the first time—every person this family disappeared, standing in the moonlit rows. The men flee. The heir collapses under the weight of being seen. Emotional beat: cathartic reversal; invisibility turned against those who wielded it.

chapters.title: Naming Him
chapters.summary: Elodie's POV. No court will convene, so she makes one: she reads Thomas's story aloud at a public meeting, with the bones documented, photographs circulated, the archive reconstructed from memory. The town must choose, again, whether to forget—and this time some refuse. Emotional beat: justice outside the law achieved through witness; truth as an act of collective refusal.

chapters.title: Returning What Was Taken
chapters.summary: Elodie's POV. She buries Thomas beside his mother's restored grave, with his real name cut in stone. The residue quiets, house by house, wall by wall. Her father, still alive and diminished, receives her silence as his sentence. Emotional beat: solemn peace; restitution as ritual rather than verdict.

chapters.title: Goodbye Is a Promise Kept
chapters.summary: Elodie and Wren's shared POV. On the Hollowmere porch, Wren's vigil ends; he held on until someone came back, and someone did. He fades not into nothing but into the ordinary world—wind, birdsong, the feeling of being watched kindly. Elodie keeps one crayon drawing. Emotional beat: bittersweet release; the friend outliving his purpose by being remembered.

chapters.title: Visible
chapters.summary: Elodie's POV, epilogue. Months later: a memorial stands, an inquiry crawls forward, and Elodie runs a pest control business that takes strange calls seriously. A child on a porch waves at someone beside her. Elodie waves back. Emotional beat: quiet transformation; she no longer needs to believe or disbelieve—only to look.
